title: Prepare thoroughly before you begin
hook: Prep can feel like dodging the real work, but a cleared desk and ready files are often what finally lets the hard task begin.
counterintuition: Preparation can waste time, and preparation can make delay harder: the difference is whether the desk, reports, and chair leave one clear first move.
tryThisNow: Before you send your next reply, move one needed document beside your keyboard. Jot the cue that made you pause and the first action it clears.
keyTakeaway: Prepare until the first move is plain: clear the desk, gather the materials, fix the comfort snag, then begin before setup becomes escape.

breakdown.fastRead:
Delaney's desk has one clean space, one report, and one pen. The rest of the pile is in a drawer until the hard task begins. That small reset changes the morning. The work still asks for effort, but it no longer starts with a search.

A ready workspace makes the first move less open to debate. Clear the desk, then begin. Gather the reports, notes, files, passwords, and reference material before the focused stretch begins. Set the chair, light, screen, and tools so your body has fewer reasons to stop. The goal is not a perfect room. The goal is a frictionless start, where the next action is so visible that delay has fewer handles.
breakdown.deepRead:
Starting often breaks on tiny snags. A missing file becomes a walk to another room. A bad chair becomes a stretch, then a snack. A crowded desk becomes a tour of unrelated duties. None of these looks like procrastination at first. Each one can feel responsible.

Adeline sees this when her usual launch turns messy. She opens the proposal file, reaches for the old report, and realizes the report is still in the shared folder. Her chair is too low, and the screen glare makes the notes hard to read. She stops before the drift begins. The work has not failed. The setup has.

She restarts in a tighter order. First the desk: only the proposal, the report, the notes, and a blank page. Then the materials: file, password, reference table, and phone number. Then the body: chair raised, lamp turned, screen cleared. The hard work is still hard, but it is no longer tangled with ten small errands.

Preparation earns its keep by ending. If Adeline keeps arranging pencils after the first sentence is ready, setup has turned into avoidance. If she gathers the report and starts the opening paragraph, setup did its job. The test is visible: did the next behavior change? A clean desk should not be a shrine. It should be a launch pad.

The same rule applies to a message, a budget, a call, or a page. Before motion begins, remove the snag that would let you stop early. Then use the clear space quickly.
breakdown.fullRead:
Holden knows the first draft failed before anyone opens the document. The evidence sits on the review table after the deadline. There were four file searches, two password resets, one charger trip, and a half hour spent reading old notes chosen too late. The task was difficult, but the stall was mostly local.

That review is useful because it keeps preparation tied to proof. The clean desk case is not about liking neat spaces. A clear surface lets one task sit where the eye can find it. When every unpaid bill, spare form, and half-read article remains in reach, each object can ask for attention. The launch pad has to be narrow.

Gathered documents teach the same lesson from another angle. The needed packet belongs in place before the work block starts: report, notes, password, file, and reference page. Searching during the block feels like work because the hands are busy and the screen is active. Yet the mind has left the frog. It is now hunting for permission to start later.

Comfort also counts. Comfort counts when it keeps you working. A chair that pinches, a lamp that throws glare, a screen at the wrong height, or a missing tool can become the first exit ramp. This is not luxury. It is removing a predictable excuse before it gets a vote.

Drew catches the error midstream in a smaller moment. He begins a client reply, then goes hunting for the report number he should have opened first. Three tabs later, he notices what he is doing. The search has become safer than the sentence. He closes the extra tabs, places the report beside the reply, and writes the first line.

That moment marks the hard edge. Preparation is useful only when it changes what happens next. A person can polish a workspace for an hour and still avoid the frog. A person can also move one file, adjust one chair, open one report, and begin. The second person is prepared. The first person is decorating delay.

Thomas's memo puts the rule in writing for his team. Choose the task, clear the surface, gather the materials, remove the comfort snag, and start while the first action is still obvious. The memo is short because the setup should be easy to repeat. A ritual that needs twenty steps becomes another task to avoid.

Laurence uses the same check before a tense reply. He moves the one client file next to the keyboard and leaves the phone across the room. The moved file is the cue. It says: answer from the record, not from irritation. One object can make the better start easier to see.

There is also a time to do the opposite. When a problem is changing fast, when facts are truly missing, or when another person is waiting for a quick human answer, more setup may be the wrong move. Send the plain reply, make the call, or ask for the missing fact. Preparation serves the start; it should not steal it.

examples.title: Delaney's Clean Thread

planSpec.audience: Delaney, a team lead clearing a desk before answering a tense message
planSpec.stakes: A cluttered desk can pull the reply toward side issues before the one task starts.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Show a clean desk launch pad through a short message exchange before action begins.

examples.scenario: Delaney's chat opens with a teammate asking, "Can you answer the client now?" Delaney replies, "One minute. Clearing the desk." The teammate asks, "For a reply?" Delaney writes, "For one reply." The invoice stack goes into a drawer. One report, one pen, and the client file stay on the clean desk. The launch pad has only the required materials.
examples.whatToDo: Delaney clears the desk before typing. She leaves only the client file, the report, and a pen where her eyes will land when the reply box opens.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows that setup can be brief and useful. The clear surface points attention toward one task before nearby objects invite other work.

examples.title: Adeline's Restart Stack

planSpec.audience: Adeline, a proposal writer rebuilding her start after a missing report interrupts her
planSpec.stakes: A missing file can turn the work block into a hunt for supplies.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Interrupt the routine, stop, gather documents, and restart differently.

examples.scenario: Adeline begins the proposal in her home office, then reaches for the old report and finds an empty folder. The routine is already fraying: shared drive, password, notes, reference table. She shuts the document instead of pretending the hunt is writing. Five minutes later the reports, notes, files, password card, and reference material sit in one stack. The second start is quieter.
examples.whatToDo: Adeline stops the broken start and rebuilds it. She gathers every document she already knows she will need, then reopens the proposal with the stack beside her.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is the technique. Gathering materials before the work block keeps retrieval from becoming a respectable way to avoid the first sentence.

examples.title: Pierce's Chair Angle

planSpec.audience: Pierce, a bookkeeper preparing for a long reconciliation task
planSpec.stakes: Discomfort can give attention another reason to quit before focus arrives.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use one close observed moment to show chair, light, screen, and tools supporting focus.

examples.scenario: Pierce's chair squeaks once when he lowers it, then the room settles. The lamp moves left so it stops shining across the screen. A calculator, pencil, and file opener line up beside the ledger. Nothing dramatic happens at the bookkeeping desk. His back stops complaining, the screen stops flashing, and the tools sit within reach before the numbers begin.
examples.whatToDo: Pierce adjusts the chair, lamp, screen, and tools before opening the ledger. He removes the discomforts he can predict.
examples.whyItMatters: Comfort is practical when it protects the first work block. Small physical snags can become excuses, so the setup should remove them early.

examples.title: Holden's Missed Materials

planSpec.audience: Holden, a project manager reviewing why a draft stalled
planSpec.stakes: Hindsight can separate hard work from avoidable searches.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Open after the outcome and reconstruct how missing materials drove the stall.

examples.scenario: Holden, the project manager, stands at Friday's project review table after the draft is already late. The table holds the evidence: four searches for reports, two missing file names, one password reset, and scattered notes from three folders. No one blames effort. The record shows that materials were fetched one by one while the hard paragraph waited.
examples.whatToDo: Holden marks each search that happened during execution and moves those reports, notes, files, and password steps into the next pre-work checklist.
examples.whyItMatters: The review turns preparation into evidence. If retrieval keeps breaking the work block, the next start needs gathered materials, not more resolve.

examples.title: Drew Catches the Hunt

planSpec.audience: Drew, an account lead noticing his own avoidance during a reply
planSpec.stakes: Searching can feel productive while the reply remains unwritten.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Let Drew notice his own error mid-stream and correct the setup before continuing.

examples.scenario: Drew starts the client reply with the cursor blinking after one weak sentence. He opens reports, notes, files, and reference material, then another tab for good measure. The mistake lands when he sees the reply still has one sentence. He is not writing; he is roaming. He closes the extra tabs, keeps the needed report open, and puts the client file beside the keyboard.
examples.whatToDo: Drew turns the client file into the only cue on the desk. He writes the next sentence from that source before he allows another search.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery happens at the moment of noticing. Searching stops being neutral once it replaces the sentence the work actually needs.

examples.title: Thomas's Launch Memo

planSpec.audience: Thomas, an operations lead writing a memo before a focused work block
planSpec.stakes: A team ritual can become too complex unless the first step stays visible.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Carry the scene through a written memo that chooses simple launch-pad preparation.

examples.scenario: Thomas, the operations lead, sends a Thursday team memo before the shared work block. It begins, "Decision for today's launch: simple setup wins." The note rejects a longer ritual. Clear the workspace, gather tools and information, fix one comfort snag, then begin immediately. If setup keeps growing after the first step is clear, start the task.
examples.whatToDo: Thomas writes the rule into the memo and keeps it short enough to repeat. The team gets a simple launch order, not another planning chore.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo protects the hard edge. A frictionless start should lower the effort to begin, not create a fresh ritual that delays action.

questions.prompt: Two writers pause before a hard proposal. One clears a report path; the other starts typing with missing files. Which response fits preparation best?
choices: The writer who types first protects momentum by skipping setup.
The writer who gathers later can treat each search as progress.
The writer who clears obstacles first makes the start less negotiable.
questions.explanation: Preparation is useful when it removes obstacles to starting. Typing first can look bold, but missing files often turn the work block into a series of exits.

questions.prompt: A desk photo shows one laptop, one folder, and one blank page. Another shows invoices, notes, and three open projects. Which setup better supports a clear first move?
choices: The clearer desk is more likely to cue single-task attention.
The busier desk is more likely to prove work has real momentum.
The fuller desk is more likely to keep useful options visible.
questions.explanation: A clear workspace strengthens attention on one task. A busy desk may show activity, but it also lets unrelated objects compete for the next glance.

questions.prompt: When a budget block begins, Adeline lacks the report, password, and reference file. Which setup would have served the block better?
choices: She could find each item later when the budget shows where to look.
She could start with memory first and confirm details after a draft.
She could gather the materials before the work block begins.
questions.explanation: Reports, notes, files, passwords, and references belong in place before the block. Gathering later fragments attention and gives delay a clean disguise.

questions.prompt: Drew has twelve tabs open and one sentence written. Which reading best explains the danger in his search?
choices: The search may be avoidance because it replaces the writing.
The search may be research because every tab could help later.
The search may be warming up because movement reduces pressure.
questions.explanation: Searching during execution can become avoidance. Drew's tabs matter less than the stalled sentence they have replaced.

questions.prompt: Pierce moves the lamp, raises the chair, and pulls tools within reach before a long ledger task. Why does that fit the lesson?
choices: It makes the workspace feel more polished before anyone judges it.
It removes physical snags that could interrupt sustained focus.
It gives her a longer warmup before the first hard number.
questions.explanation: Physical comfort supports sustained focus. The chair, lamp, screen, and tools matter when they prevent predictable reasons to stop.

questions.prompt: A teammate spends forty minutes improving the setup after the first action is already clear. Which judgment fits the hard edge?
choices: The setup is still useful because more care usually protects quality.
The setup has become procrastination because it never turns into action.
The setup should expand because serious work deserves a richer ritual.
questions.explanation: Preparation becomes procrastination when it never turns into action. Once the next move is clear, more arranging can become a softer form of delay.

questions.prompt: Your first move is written on a card beside the file, while your motivation still feels low. Which conclusion best follows?
choices: The ready first step lowers the effort needed to begin.
The low motivation means the first step should wait.
The card matters mainly as proof that planning happened.
questions.explanation: A ready first step lowers activation energy. Motivation can stay imperfect; the visible next act makes starting less dependent on mood.

questions.prompt: One phone sits beside a blank reply, and one client file sits beside the keyboard. Which cue best serves the chosen task?
choices: The nearby phone serves the task because it keeps every message in view.
The blank reply serves the task because pressure alone can force focus.
The client file serves the task because it points attention at the reply.
questions.explanation: Environmental cues should point toward the chosen task. A file beside the keyboard supports the reply; the phone may invite other messages.

questions.prompt: A launch routine has twenty steps and needs its own checklist. What should be changed first?
choices: Add more setup steps so the routine feels serious enough.
Simplify the setup so it can be repeated before real work.
Save the routine for rare days when the task feels important.
questions.explanation: The setup should be simple enough to repeat. A complex ritual adds a new barrier, which works against a frictionless start.

reviewCards.front: What is a frictionless start in plain terms?
reviewCards.back: It is a setup that clears the desk, gathers needed materials, removes a comfort snag, and leaves the first action visible before focused work begins.

reviewCards.front: Why does the clean desk work as a launch pad?
reviewCards.back: A clean desk limits the visual claims on your attention. When only the required materials remain, the surface cues one task instead of several small escapes.

reviewCards.front: How do gathered documents stop a work block from breaking apart?
reviewCards.back: Reports, notes, files, passwords, and references are ready before execution. The work block can stay on the frog instead of becoming a search session.
It becomes procrastination when the next action is clear but setup keeps growing. Preparation has to end in a visible start, not a nicer delay.

reviewCards.front: Why do chair, light, screen, and tools belong in the lesson?
reviewCards.back: They matter because discomfort can become a reason to stop. Fixing the obvious snag before work begins protects focus during the first hard stretch.

reviewCards.front: Recall goal clarity before action (Ch 1): where does a written result change setup here?
reviewCards.back: It changes setup when the chosen result tells you which report, file, chair fix, or first sentence belongs on the launch pad. Without that result, clean can drift into busy.

implementationPlan.title: Stage the First Move
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making the first action visible before you begin hard work. Stage the First Move by clearing the surface, gathering the exact materials, fixing one comfort snag, and starting while the next step is still plain. The skill is not neatness; it is ending setup in action.

ifThenPlans.context: The task feels hard to start
ifThenPlans.plan: If the task feels hard to start, then move one needed object into view and name the first action it clears.

ifThenPlans.context: A file or password will probably be needed
ifThenPlans.plan: If you can predict a needed report, note, file, password, or reference, then gather it before the work block begins.

ifThenPlans.context: Your body is already resisting the work spot
ifThenPlans.plan: If the chair, light, screen, or tool position is bothering you, then fix one snag before you open the hard task.

ifThenPlans.context: The first action is clear but setup keeps growing
ifThenPlans.plan: If the first action is clear and you are still arranging, then stop the setup and begin the named action.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, before you send your next response about a hard task, move one needed object beside your keyboard. Write one line naming the cue, object, and first action.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one person this week to flag moments when your setup keeps growing after the first move is clear. Compare notes once and pick one object cue to keep.

memorableLines.why: It turns the clean desk case into a plain action rule.

memorableLines.text: Preparation earns its keep by ending.
memorableLines.why: It gives preparation a clean test against procrastination.

memorableLines.text: Comfort counts when it keeps you working.
memorableLines.why: It makes the chair and light case practical instead of indulgent.
